{{distinguish|Generalised metric}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[category theory]], a '''generalized metric space''' is a [[metric space]] but without some properties, such as [[symmetric relation|symmetry]].<ref>Namely, the property that distinct elements have non-zero [[metric space|distance]] between them and the property that the distance between two elements is always finite.</ref> Precisely, it is a category [[enriched category|enriched]] over <math>[0, \infty]</math>, the [[one-point compactification]] of <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. The notion was introduced in 1973 by [[William Lawvere]] who noticed that a metric space can be viewed as a particular kind of category.

The categorical point of view is useful since by [[Yoneda's lemma]], a generalized metric space can be embedded into a much larger category in which, for instance, one can construct the [[Cauchy completion (category theory)|Cauchy completion]] of the space.

== Discussion ==
We can view <math>\overline{\mathbb{R}}_+ = [0, \infty]</math> as a [[symmetric monoidal category]] as follows:{{sfnp|Lawvere|1973|loc=§ 1|p=145}} objects are points in <math>\overline{\mathbb{R}}_+</math>, the set of morphisms between objects <math>a, b</math> is
:<math> \operatorname{Hom}(a, b) = \begin{cases}
\{ b - a \}, & \text{if } b \geq a, \\
\quad\;\varnothing, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}</math>
and composition <math>\circ: \operatorname{Hom}(b, c) \times \operatorname{Hom}(a, b) \to \operatorname{Hom}(c, a)</math> is given by the sum
:<math>(\{ c - b \}, \{ b - a \}) \mapsto \{ c - b + b - a \}.</math>
The tensor operation is <math>a \otimes b = a + b</math>. 

This category structure is equivalent to one obtained by viewing the poset <math>(\overline{\mathbb{R}}_+, \ge)</math> as a category in the usual way. The above definition is analogous to the following example: let <math>M</math> be the Boolean algebra generated by some subsets of a [[finite set]] and with <math>a \to b := b \supset a</math> and with <math>a \otimes b := a \cup b</math>. Then <math>M</math> is a symmetric monoidal category.

Now, let <math>(X, d)</math> be a metric space. Then it can be viewed as a category enriched over <math>\overline{\mathbb{R}}_+</math> as follows. The objects are the points of <math>X</math> and we let <math>\operatorname{Hom}(x, y) = d(x, y)</math>. The composition for <math>x, y, z</math> is a morphism in <math>\overline{\mathbb{R}}_+</math>
:<math>\circ: \operatorname{Hom}(y, z) \otimes \operatorname{Hom}(x, y) \to \operatorname{Hom}(x, z)</math>
and its well-definedness is exactly the [[triangle inequality]].
